1.title: Exam Orientation and How to Study
1.text: Welcome to Module zero: Exam Orientation and How to Study. Each part of this module comes from the study notes of the same name, so you can read the notes after you watch.

1.title: What You Will Learn
1.text: By the end of this module you will be able to do six things. The exam at a glance. The four learning outcomes and their weights. Pass strategy and the open book. The five-step method for a classic question. Project Harbor and a study plan. Practice with exam-style questions and a recall check.

1.title: Where This Fits in the Exam
1.text: Here is where this module sits in the exam. Scope: All learning outcomes: exam format, weights and method. Exam format: an open-book scenario exam: one hundred fifty minutes, seventy marks, forty-two marks to pass. Validated against: the official prince two seven Practitioner syllabus (people cert), version seven point two.

1.title: The exam at a glance
1.text: The exam at a glance. The Practitioner exam does not test whether you can recall the method. It tests whether you can apply it to a project scenario and analyze whether an action is appropriate.

1.title: The exam at a glance, continued
1.text: The exam at a glance. The figure shows this: The exam map: scenario, additional information and questions, with the four learning outcomes and their weights.

1.title: The exam at a glance, continued
1.text: The exam at a glance. Book. Open book: the Official Book, which you may annotate; no other material. Time. one hundred fifty minutes; one hundred eighty-eight minutes if the exam is not in your native or working language. Marks. seventy marks, one mark per part question, no negative marking. Pass mark. forty-two of seventy (sixty percent). Thinking. Bloom three (apply to a situation) and Bloom four (analyze whether an action is effective). Format. A Project Scenario, Additional Information about people, and the questions.

1.title: The exam at a glance, continued
1.text: The exam at a glance. The Additional Information describes people who work on the project. At least one question needs it, so read it every time a question names a person. Classic. What you see: A short situation, a question and four options A to D; often "Was this an appropriate action, and why?" with two "Yes, because" and two "No, because" options. Marks: one mark.

1.title: The exam at a glance, continued
1.text: The exam at a glance. Matching. What you see: Three pieces of information and a list of five or six options; match each piece to one option; an option may be used once, more than once or not at all. Marks: three marks, one for each part.

1.title: The exam at a glance, continued
1.text: The exam at a glance. Each of the three parts is marked on its own, so a partly right matching answer still earns marks. Exam tip: In a classic question, decide yes or no first, then choose the reason. Two options share your decision; only one of them gives a reason that fits the facts in the scenario.

1.title: The four learning outcomes and their weights
1.text: The four learning outcomes and their weights. one. Principles in context. Weight: ten percent. About (of seventy marks): seven. Modules: one. two. People management. Weight: nine percent. About (of seventy marks): six. Modules: two. three. Practices in context. Weight: fifty-one percent. About (of seventy marks): thirty-six. Modules: three to nine. four. Processes in context. Weight: thirty percent. About (of seventy marks): twenty-one. Modules: ten to sixteen. Each practice and each process has two criteria. Apply (Bloom three): the management products, the areas of focus of the key roles, and effective management and techniques (practices); or the activities, inputs, outputs and roles (processes). Analyze (Bloom four): is the approach effective and fit for purpose, considering the principles, the techniques and tailoring? This is the harder kind. Exam tip: The seven practices are fifty-one percent of the marks, and with the processes you reach eighty-one percent. Put most of your study time there.

1.title: Pass strategy and the open book
1.text: Pass strategy and the open book. one hundred fifty minutes for seventy marks is a little over two minutes per mark (about two point seven with one hundred eighty-eight minutes). A matching question has three marks, so give it about five minutes.

1.title: Pass strategy and the open book, continued
1.text: Pass strategy and the open book. First pass. Answer every classic question you can in about two minutes. Mark and return. If a question needs over three minutes, choose the best option, mark it and move on. Reserve time. Keep about fifteen minutes at the end for marked questions. Never leave a blank. There is no negative marking, so a guess costs nothing. Pass arithmetic. forty-two of seventy lets you miss twenty-eight part questions. How to use the open book.

1.title: Pass strategy and the open book, continued
1.text: Pass strategy and the open book. Annotate. Write short cues beside each practice's roles table, product list and tailoring section. Tab. Mark every principle, people, practice and process section and each roles table. Know where things are. Practice finding any table in under thirty seconds. Do not rely on reading. A chapter takes minutes you do not have; the book confirms a detail. Check the rules. Read people cert's current candidate rules on what may be added to the book. Exam tip: Use the book to confirm, not to learn. If you must read a whole section to understand a question, mark it and move on.

1.title: The five-step method for a classic question
1.text: The five-step method for a classic question. Read the scenario and the last line. Note the stage, the names, the numbers and any tolerance. If a person is named, check the Additional Information. Find the process or practice. Which process is the project in, and which practice owns the topic? Check roles and authority. Who may decide, who approves, who must only be told? Check tolerances and principles. Inside tolerance the project manager acts; a forecast breach goes up. Does the action break a principle?

1.title: The five-step method for a classic question, continued
1.text: The five-step method for a classic question. Choose the option whose reason is right, not only whose action is right. Two options often share the right action and differ in the reason. Worked example. In the build stage of Project Harbor, Sam Okafor forecasts a cost overrun of three percent against a stage tolerance of plus or minus ten percent. He deals with it inside the stage and notes it in the next highlight report. Was this appropriate?

1.title: The five-step method for a classic question, continued
1.text: The five-step method for a classic question. Step two: controlling a stage. Step three: the project manager has the authority. Step four: inside tolerance, so manage by exception. Step five: "Yes, because it is within tolerance and so within delegated authority.". For a matching question, apply the method to each part separately. Options can be reused, so never cross one off after using it. Exam tip: The reason decides the mark. If two options both say "Yes", compare the "because" clauses with the scenario facts and the role's authority.

1.title: Project Harbor and a study plan
1.text: Project Harbor and a study plan. Scenarios in this course use one fictional project. Project. Brightwater Port Authority replaces its paper berth-permit process with an online permit service. Budget and time. four hundred eighty thousand and nine months. Stages. Initiation, build, pilot, rollout. Board. Marta Quinn, executive (director of operations); Tomas Reyes, senior user (harbor master); Lena Kovac, senior supplier (account director, Delta Software). Management. Sam Okafor, project manager; Wei Chen, team manager (Delta Software's developers).

2.title: Project Harbor and a study plan, continued
2.text: Project Harbor and a study plan. Support roles. Aisha Bello, project assurance (finance business partner); Jon Park, project support; Tomas Reyes also has the delegated authority for small changes. Tolerances. Typically plus or minus ten percent cost and plus or minus two weeks time per stage.

2.title: Project Harbor and a study plan, continued
2.text: Project Harbor and a study plan. A six-week plan. one. Modules: zero to two. Focus: Exam method, principles, people. two. Modules: three to five. Focus: Business case, organization, plans. three. Modules: six to nine. Focus: Quality, risk, issues, progress. four. Modules: ten to thirteen. Focus: Starting up, directing, initiating, controlling a stage. five. Modules: fourteen to sixteen. Focus: Managing product delivery, stage boundary, closing. six. Modules: seventeen. Focus: Timed practice, weak spots, book tabs. For each module: read the note, read the matching Official Book pages (roles table, products, tailoring), annotate them, then answer the questions with the book closed and check every miss.

2.title: Practice Question 1
2.text: Question one. A candidate in the one hundred fifty-minute exam spends six minutes on one classic question, then picks the better option, marks it and moves on. Was this appropriate, and why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: Yes, because a marked best guess saves time for other questions. The method is to mark and return, and since there is no negative marking a best guess costs nothing while the time saved earns marks elsewhere.

2.title: Practice Question 2
2.text: Question two. In a matching question on Project Harbor, a candidate matches part one to the senior user, crosses that role off, and so cannot use it for part two, which also fits. Was this appropriate, and why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is D: No, because options may be used once, more than once or not at all. Matching options can be reused or left unused, so crossing one off throws away a correct answer.

2.title: Practice Question 3
2.text: Question three. During preparation a candidate writes short cues beside the roles table of each practice in the Official Book, so each table can be found in seconds. Was this appropriate, and why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is B: Yes, because the book may be annotated and quick lookup saves time. The open-book rule allows notes inside the book, and fast lookup helps confirm a detail without reading whole chapters.

2.title: Practice Question 4
2.text: Question four. A candidate has six weeks and wants study time to follow the marks. Which plan fits the weights best? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: Most time on practices, then processes, then principles and people. Practices carry fifty-one percent and processes thirty percent, so they should take most of the time, while principles are ten percent and people nine percent.

2.title: Practice Question 5
2.text: Question five. A question asks how Sam Okafor should tell Lena Kovac about a delay. Where should the candidate look for her communication preferences? The four options are on the screen. The answer is A: In the Additional Information about the people on the project. The Additional Information gives facts about named people, and at least one question depends on it.

2.title: Practice Question 6
2.text: Question six. A candidate leaves one part of a matching question blank to avoid losing a mark. Was this appropriate, and why? The four options are on the screen. The answer is C: No, because wrong answers cost nothing and each part earns a mark. Each part is a one-mark part question and wrong answers cost nothing, so a blank can only lose marks.

2.title: Recall Check 1
2.text: Recall check one. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question one. What is the pass mark? Answer: forty-two of seventy marks (sixty percent). Question two. How long is the exam, and how long with extra time? Answer: one hundred fifty minutes; one hundred eighty-eight minutes if the exam is not in your native or working language. Question three. What are the weights of the four learning outcomes? Answer: Principles ten percent, people nine percent, practices fifty-one percent and processes thirty percent.

2.title: Recall Check 2
2.text: Recall check two. Say each answer out loud before you listen to mine. Question four. Which Bloom levels does the exam use? Answer: Level three (apply) and level four (analyze). Question five. How many marks is a matching question worth, and may options repeat? Answer: Three marks, one per part; options may be used once, more than once or not at all. Question six. What is the fifth step of the method for a classic question? Answer: Choose the option whose reason is right, not only whose action is right.

2.title: Module Recap
2.text: Here is the recap. Format: open book (the Official Book, annotated); one hundred fifty minutes, one hundred eighty-eight with extra time; seventy marks. Thinking: Bloom three apply and Bloom four analyze, on a scenario with Additional Information about people. Question types: classic (one mark, four options) and matching (three marks, reusable options). Weights: principles ten percent, people nine percent, practices fifty-one percent, processes thirty percent. Time: about two minutes per mark; mark and return; keep fifteen minutes. Open book: annotate, tab, know the tables; confirm, do not learn. Method: scenario, process or practice, roles and authority, tolerances and principles, right reason.
